225.title: The last two of al-Baqarah
225.hook: our Lord, do not burden us beyond what we can bear (2:285–286)
225.howItsDone: Many Muslims recite the last two verses of Surah al-Baqarah (2:285–286) each night before sleep, following the hadith that they suffice whoever recites them; the pleas of 2:286 are also said as a du'a on their own.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ayat al-Kursi: the Living, the Sustainer, untouched by drowsiness. Your line was he does not sleep. Did you put the day down last night before you slept? Day two hundred twenty-five.

Have you ever read a rule and felt your stomach drop? Not because you wanted to break it, but because you knew you couldn't keep it. That's what happened to the companions of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ near the end of Surah al-Baqarah. A verse came saying that whether you show what's in yourselves or hide it, Allah will bring you to account for it. What's in yourselves. The thoughts you never chose. Sahih Muslim records that they came to the Prophet and fell to their knees: this is more than we can bear. What happened next gave us two verses that millions of people say every single night. Today: the last two of al-Baqarah.
screen: `A VERSE THAT FELT TOO HEAVY.` → `ON THEIR KNEES: MORE THAN WE CAN BEAR.` → `WHAT CAME NEXT.`

segments.voice: The Prophet told them not to turn away but to say: we hear and we obey; Your forgiveness, our Lord, and to You is the return. They said it, and the words came back to them as scripture. Verse two eighty-five describes the messenger and the believers who believe in Allah, His angels, His books and His messengers, and who say exactly that: we hear and we obey, Your forgiveness, our Lord. Then verse two eighty-six opens with the answer to their fear. Pickthall translates: Allah tasketh not a soul beyond its scope. Scope, in Arabic wus', means capacity, width, room. You are asked for what you have room for. Each soul gets what it earned, and bears what it did. Then the verse becomes a list of pleas, the ones the companions made on their knees. Our Lord, don't take us to task if we forget or make mistakes. Don't lay on us a burden like the ones laid on those before us. Don't load us with what we have no strength for. Pardon us, forgive us, have mercy on us. You are our Protector. The report in Sahih Muslim adds a detail people love: after each plea, Allah answered, I have done so. The worry about thoughts you never chose is answered too: other hadith say a person isn't held to account for passing thoughts they don't act on or speak. And Bukhari records the Prophet saying that whoever recites these last two verses at night, they will be enough for him. The heaviest verse of the surah, followed by its gentlest ending.
screen: `WE HEAR AND WE OBEY.` · `WUS' — CAPACITY, ROOM.` · `DON'T TAKE US TO TASK IF WE FORGET.` · `I HAVE DONE SO.` · then, large: `NOT BEYOND WHAT WE BEAR.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think of what you're carrying right now. Not the whole list. Just the heaviest thing. Feel where it sits in your body: the chest, the shoulders, the stomach. Now breathe into that place and hear the line: not beyond its scope. Whatever else is true about this weight, the verse says it isn't bigger than the room you've been given. If you pray, you can recite the last two verses of al-Baqarah tonight, or just their pleas, one on each breath. The bell holds the time.
The last two of al-Baqarah. Verses two eighty-five and six: we hear and we obey, and Allah tasks no soul beyond its scope. Today's word.
screen: `THE LAST TWO OF AL-BAQARAH — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: not beyond what we bear. When something feels like too much today, say it to yourself once, and then do only the next small part. Day two hundred twenty-five.

226.title: Al-Fatiha, again
226.hook: the mother of the book, now heard with thirty surahs behind it
226.howItsDone: Muslims recite al-Fatiha in every unit of every prayer, at least seventeen times a day in the obligatory prayers, and also at weddings, over the sick, and in remembrance of the dead; many learn its meaning line by line to recite it with attention.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last two of al-Baqarah: Allah tasks no soul beyond its scope. Your line was not beyond what we bear. When something felt like too much, did you do only the next small part? Day two hundred twenty-six.

Some songs you heard as a kid mean something completely different when you hear them at forty. The words haven't changed. You have. Back in the first weeks of this path, we met the Fatiha, the opening, seven short lines said in every unit of every prayer. You learned them as a beginner learns them: one phrase at a time. Since then you've read the whole last part of the Qur'an. The Day of sorting. The orphan. The whisperer. The Living who does not sleep. So today we go back to the start and hear the same seven lines again, with thirty-seven surahs standing behind them. Today: the mother of the book.
screen: `THE SAME SONG AT FORTY.` → `SEVEN LINES, MET AS A BEGINNER.` → `HEARD AGAIN, WITH A JUZ' BEHIND THEM.`

segments.voice: Bukhari records the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ calling the Fatiha umm al-Qur'an, the mother of the Qur'an, and the seven oft-repeated verses. Umm al-kitab: the mother of the book. In Arabic, umm is a mother, and also a source, the thing that gathers everything around it. The capital of a region can be called its umm. Now listen with the juz' behind you. Here is Pickthall: Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds, The Beneficent, the Merciful. Owner of the Day of Judgment. Lord of the worlds: An-Naba' pointed at the earth as a bed and the mountains as pegs. That's the lordship, spread out. The Beneficent, the Merciful: nearly every surah opened with those two names. Owner of the Day of Judgment: the Day of sorting, the trumpet, what the hands sent ahead. Then: Thee alone we worship, Thee alone we ask for help. And show us the straight path. The juz' spent pages on that path: purify the soul, feed the orphan, don't push anyone away. The Fatiha is the whole book folded small, and the book is the Fatiha unfolded. There's one more thing that turns the Fatiha from a text into a conversation. In a hadith qudsi recorded by Muslim, Allah says He has divided the prayer between Himself and His servant. When the servant says, praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds, Allah says: My servant has praised Me. At each line, an answer. Every time it's recited, someone is replying.
screen: `UMM — MOTHER, SOURCE, GATHERER.` · `LORD, MERCIFUL, OWNER OF THE DAY.` · `THE BOOK FOLDED SMALL.` · `AT EACH LINE, AN ANSWER.` · then, large: `THE MOTHER OF THE BOOK.`

segments.voice: Sit, and take the Fatiha slowly, one line per breath, in Arabic or in English, whichever you have. Breathe in. Say the line in your mind. Breathe out. Then, before the next line, leave a small silence, the space where the hadith says an answer comes. You don't need to hear anything. Just leave the room for it. Praise, then a pause. Mercy, then a pause. The Day, then a pause. If you pray, you can let today's prayers go a little slower at the Fatiha. The bell holds the time.
Umm al-kitab. The mother of the book, a name for the Fatiha: the source that gathers the whole Qur'an into seven lines. Today's word.
Your line: the mother of the book. The next time you hear or say the Fatiha today, listen for one surah from the juz' hiding inside one of its lines. Day two hundred twenty-six.

227.title: The three quls
227.hook: Ikhlas, Falaq, Nas recited three times morning and evening (Abu Dawud)
227.howItsDone: Many Muslims recite al-Ikhlas, al-Falaq and an-Nas three times after the dawn and sunset prayers as part of their morning and evening remembrances, and before sleep into cupped hands, wiping them over the body.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Fatiha again, heard with the juz' behind it. Your line was the mother of the book. Did you hear a surah hiding inside one of its lines? Day two hundred twenty-seven.

A dark night in Medina, rain coming down hard, the kind of dark where you can't see your own hand. A small group of men go out looking for the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, hoping he'll lead them in prayer. They find him. One of them, Abdullah ibn Khubayb, tells what happened next, and Abu Dawud records it. The Prophet turned to him and said one word: say. Abdullah said nothing. Say. Nothing. A third time: say. Finally Abdullah asked, what should I say? And the answer is three short surahs you already know, and a number. Today: the three quls.
screen: `RAIN, AND A DARK NIGHT.` → `SAY. SAY. SAY.` → `WHAT SHOULD I SAY?`

segments.voice: The Prophet told him: say Qul huwa Allahu ahad and the two surahs of refuge, three times in the evening and three times in the morning, and they will be enough for you against everything. Three surahs, three times, twice a day. Qul is the Arabic for say, and each of the three begins with it. Pickthall: Say: He is Allah, the One! Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the Daybreak. Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind. That's why people call them the three quls, the three says. Some also count a fourth, al-Kafirun, which begins the same way. Here's the curious part. Qul is a command to the Prophet: say this. But when Muslims recite, they keep the word. They don't just say, He is Allah, the One. They say, say: He is Allah, the One. The command is part of the revelation, so it stays. Every recitation repeats the moment of being told. Now notice how the three fit together. The first, al-Ikhlas, is about who Allah is: One, needing nothing, with no equal. The Prophet said it equals a third of the Qur'an. The second and third, al-Falaq and an-Nas, are the mu'awwidhatayn, the two refuge-takers: refuge from the dark outside, the envier and the night, and refuge from the whisperer inside. First, who you turn to. Then, what you're turning away from. And we met the other practice at the start of this camp: the Prophet would recite all three into cupped hands before sleep and wipe them over his body.
screen: `QUL — SAY.` · `THE COMMAND STAYS IN THE RECITING.` · `WHO YOU TURN TO, THEN WHAT FROM.` · `MORNING AND EVENING, THREE EACH.` · then, large: `THREE TIMES, THREE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your hands rest open on your knees. Think of the day's two edges, the morning when you step out and the evening when you come back in. Picture yourself at the door at each one. What would you like to be held by as you go out? What would you like to be kept from as you come home? If you pray, you can recite the three quls now, once each, slowly, and again three times tonight. If you don't, sit with the first line, He is One, on each breath. The bell holds the time.
The three quls. Al-Ikhlas, al-Falaq and an-Nas, the three surahs that begin with say, recited three times at morning and at evening. Today's word.
Your line: three times, three. Tonight, before sleep, say or read the three quls, each three times, and notice how long it really takes. Under two minutes. Day two hundred twenty-seven.

228.title: Tajwid, a first taste
228.hook: recitation has rules of sound: stretching, nasal hums, stops
228.carry: every letter is due its right
228.howItsDone: Muslims learn tajwid from a teacher, usually by ear and repetition, often in mosque classes or with a local reciter; advanced students may receive an ijazah, a license to teach recitation, with a chain of teachers going back many generations.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the three quls: say, say, say, three times at morning and evening. Your line was three times, three. How long did it really take last night? Day two hundred twenty-eight.

Put on a recording of the Qur'an recited well, and listen for a minute without trying to understand a word. You'll notice it isn't quite singing, and it isn't quite speaking. Some vowels stretch, long and steady, like a held note. Some sounds hum in the nose for a beat. Then the voice stops, exactly, and breathes, and starts again. It sounds free, but it isn't improvised. Every one of those stretches and hums follows a rule, and the rules have been handed down, teacher to student, for centuries. Children in Cairo and Jakarta and Chicago learn the same ones. Today: tajwid, a first taste.
screen: `NOT SINGING, NOT SPEAKING.` → `STRETCHES, HUMS AND STOPS.` → `RULES HANDED DOWN.`

segments.voice: Tajwid comes from the root j-w-d, to make good, to make excellent. Jayyid, good, is from the same root. So tajwid is making the recitation good: giving the words the sound they were given in. The classical manuals define it with a line that became our carry: giving every letter its right and its due. Its right is how it's made: where in the throat, the tongue, the lips or the nose each letter lives. Its due is what happens to it next to other letters. Three rules make a first taste. One, madd, stretching. A long vowel is held for two beats, and in some places four or six. Listen to the end of the Fatiha, wa lad-daaaallin: that long a is held for six. Two, ghunnah, the nasal hum. When a noon or a meem is doubled, as in inna, the sound rests in the nose for two beats. Three, waqf, stopping. Small marks above the line tell the reciter where a stop is required, where it's allowed, and where stopping would bend the meaning. The Qur'an itself asks for this care: in Surah al-Muzzammil, recite the Qur'an with tartil, measured and distinct. Scholars say avoiding mistakes that change meaning is required; the finer rules are a craft, learned by ear from a teacher, often with a chain of teachers going back generations. And here is the kindest hadith for beginners. Bukhari and Muslim record the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ saying that the one skilled in the Qur'an is with the noble, righteous scribes, and the one who stumbles through it, finding it hard, gets two rewards.
screen: `J-W-D — TO MAKE EXCELLENT.` · `MADD — THE STRETCH.` · `GHUNNAH — THE HUM.` · `WAQF — THE STOP.` · then, large: `EVERY LETTER IS DUE ITS RIGHT.`

segments.voice: Sit, and just listen inwardly. Say the word Allah slowly in your mind, or aloud if you're alone, and notice the long a in the middle. Let it stretch, two beats, like a breath held gently. Then hum, mmm, with your lips closed, and feel where it sits: in the nose, behind the face. That's the place ghunnah lives. Then stop, completely, and let the silence be exact. Stretch, hum, stop. Do it a few times, slowly, as if every sound had a right to be heard in full. The bell holds the time.
Tajwid. Making excellent: the rules of Qur'an recitation, the stretch, the hum and the stop, so every letter gets its right. Today's word.

Your line: every letter is due its right. Today, listen to one short recitation, and catch one stretched vowel, the held note. Then, in one conversation, give someone's words their full length before you answer. Day two hundred twenty-eight.

229.title: Your own voice
229.hook: the Prophet ﷺ liked to hear the Qur'an from others (Bukhari)
229.howItsDone: Muslims recite the Qur'an aloud in prayer, in study circles, and at home; many listen to well-known reciters, and teachers encourage students to recite in their own voice with care and feeling rather than imitating a performance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tajwid: the stretch, the hum and the stop. Your line was every letter is due its right. Did you catch one held vowel, or let someone finish their sentence? Day two hundred twenty-nine.

Most of us hate hearing our own voice. On a voicemail, in a video, it sounds thin and strange, not like us at all. So yesterday's rules might leave you thinking the Qur'an belongs to the professionals, the famous reciters with voices like cellos. But there's a story in Bukhari that turns this upside down. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, the one the Qur'an was revealed to, turned to a companion and asked him to recite. The companion was baffled. Recite to you? It was sent down to you. And the Prophet said: I like to hear it from someone else. Today: your own voice.
screen: `WE HATE HEARING OUR OWN VOICE.` → `RECITE TO YOU?` → `I LIKE TO HEAR IT FROM SOMEONE ELSE.`

segments.voice: The companion was Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, a former shepherd, small and thin, whom people sometimes teased for his skinny legs. He began reciting Surah an-Nisa'. He reached the verse that asks how it will be when a witness is brought from every people, and the Prophet himself is brought as witness over them. The Prophet said: enough. Ibn Mas'ud looked up and saw tears running from his eyes. The one who received the words was moved by hearing them in another man's voice. Other reports make the same point from different sides. The Prophet heard Abu Musa al-Ash'ari reciting one night and told him he'd been given a flute, a mizmar, like those of the family of the prophet Dawud, David, famous for his singing. And in Abu Dawud's collection the Prophet says: beautify the Qur'an with your voices. Zayyinu, make it lovely. Not your voice made lovely by the Qur'an: the Qur'an made lovely by your voice. Scholars have long discussed what that allows. Most say a beautiful, moving voice is praised, as long as the tajwid is kept and the recitation doesn't turn into a performance of songs. Another hadith says he is not of us who doesn't recite the Qur'an with taghanni, a word some read as chanting it melodiously and others as being content with it. Either way, the invitation is plain. The beauty isn't only in the famous voices. It's in the ordinary voice that's trying, the one you're a little embarrassed by.
screen: `IBN MAS'UD RECITES, THE PROPHET WEEPS.` · `ABU MUSA'S FLUTE.` · `ZAYYINU — MAKE IT LOVELY.` · `THE ORDINARY VOICE THAT TRIES.` · then, large: `BEAUTIFY IT WITH YOUR VOICE.`

segments.voice: Find a spot where you can be heard only by yourself. Choose something short: the bismillah, the first line of the Fatiha, or one verse in English if that's what you have. Take a breath. Now say it out loud, once, slowly, at a normal volume. Not a whisper. Let your voice be exactly what it is. Then sit in the quiet after it and notice how it felt to hear it in your own voice rather than someone else's. If you'd like, say it once more, a little slower. The bell holds the time.
Your own voice. The Prophet liked to hear the Qur'an from others, and told people to beautify it with their voices. Today's word.
Your line: beautify it with your voice. Once today, say one line you love out loud, to no one but yourself, and let it be heard in your own voice. Day two hundred twenty-nine.

230.title: The verse you keep
230.hook: choose one verse from the juz' to carry for good
230.howItsDone: Many Muslims keep favorite verses close: written in calligraphy on walls, memorized to recite in hard moments, or repeated in night prayer; some return to one verse again and again, as the Prophet is reported to have done.

segments.voice: Yesterday, your own voice: Ibn Mas'ud reciting, and the Prophet in tears. Your line was beautify it with your voice. Did you say one line out loud, just to yourself? Day two hundred thirty.

Think of someone who keeps a note folded in their wallet for years. A line from a letter, a thing a teacher once said. The paper goes soft at the creases. They don't read it every day. They just know it's there, and on the worst days they take it out. One night, Abu Dharr reports, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ stood in prayer and recited a single verse, over and over, until dawn. One verse, a whole night. You've now read thirty-seven surahs. Tomorrow this camp closes. Before it does, there's one thing to take with you: not the whole juz', but one verse from it, kept like that folded note. Today: the verse you keep.
screen: `A NOTE FOLDED IN A WALLET.` → `ONE VERSE, A WHOLE NIGHT.` → `ONE VERSE TO TAKE WITH YOU.`

segments.voice: Early Muslims learned the Qur'an slowly. An early report says the companions would take ten verses at a time and not move on until they knew them and had lived them. A kept verse works the same way: not a quotation to admire, but a line that does a job in your life. Here are three that many Muslims keep, from the part we've read. From Ash-Sharh, Surah ninety-four, in Pickthall: But lo! with hardship goeth ease, Lo! with hardship goeth ease. Notice two things. The word is with, ma'a, not after: the ease is already inside the hard thing, not only waiting beyond it. And the line is said twice. Commentators noticed that hardship has the definite article, the hardship, while ease does not, so they read it as one hardship and two eases. A report from Ibn Abbas puts it: one hardship will not overcome two eases. From Ad-Duha, Surah ninety-three, words to the Prophet in a dry season when revelation had paused: your Lord has not forsaken you, nor does He hate you. And from Az-Zalzalah, Surah ninety-nine: And whoso doeth good an atom's weight will see it then. Nothing is too small to count. One for the hard day, one for the lonely day, one for the ordinary day. But the verse you keep doesn't have to be any of these. It might be the whisperer that withdraws, or sleep as a sign. The only test is whether you'll take it out when you need it.
screen: `TEN VERSES AT A TIME.` · `WITH HARDSHIP, EASE — SAID TWICE.` · `NOT FORSAKEN.` · `AN ATOM'S WEIGHT OF GOOD.` · then, large: `ONE VERSE, KEPT.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the verses of these weeks pass through your mind like cards being shuffled. Don't pick the one that sounds most impressive. Wait for the one that pulls at you, the one that seems to know something about your life right now. When it comes, hold it. Say it silently on the in-breath, and let it settle on the out-breath. If you like, imagine folding it small and putting it somewhere safe inside you. The bell holds the time.
The verse you keep. One line from the juz', chosen, written down and carried, the way the Prophet once kept one verse through a whole night. Today's word.
Your line: one verse, kept. Today, write your verse down by hand, on paper, and put it somewhere you'll see it: a wallet, a mirror, a phone case. Day two hundred thirty.

231.title: Camp 4 close: the thirtieth part
231.hook: the part every Muslim child knows is now yours too
231.howItsDone: Muslim children usually memorize Juz' 'Amma first, from An-Nas backward, with a teacher at a mosque, a weekend school or at home; in many families finishing it is marked with a small celebration.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the verse you keep: with hardship, ease, or whichever line pulled at you. Your line was one verse, kept. Where did you put it, and have you looked at it yet? Day two hundred thirty-one.

Somewhere right now, a seven-year-old is sitting cross-legged on a mosque carpet, rocking slightly, reciting Qul a'udhu bi rabbin-nas for the hundredth time while a teacher listens with one ear and corrects with one finger. Tomorrow it'll be the next surah. In a few years, the whole last part. It's the same in Karachi, Lagos, Istanbul, Detroit. The children don't start with the long surahs at the front of the book. They start at the end, with the short ones, and work backward. That's exactly what you've done for seventy-five days. Today this camp closes, and the part every Muslim child knows is now yours too. Today: the thirtieth part.
screen: `A CHILD ON A MOSQUE CARPET.` → `STARTING FROM THE END.` → `SEVENTY-FIVE DAYS, THE SAME ROAD.`

segments.voice: Look back at the road. We began by hearing before reading: tilawah, the Qur'an as something recited aloud before it was ever a book on a shelf. Then ta'awwudh, taking refuge before you begin. Then An-Nas, the whisperer who withdraws, and from there backward, surah by surah. Al-Ikhlas and the One, ahad. Al-Kawthar's abundance. Al-Ma'un's small kindnesses. By time, people are in loss. The earth telling its news. Al-Qadr, peace until dawn. Read, the first word ever revealed. With hardship, ease. The orphan, again and again. The soul at peace, returning. Al-Wadud, the Loving. The buried girl who will be asked. The man who frowned, and was corrected. Until An-Naba', the great news, where the juz' begins. Then we carried it: into prayer, into sleep with Ayat al-Kursi, into the Fatiha heard fresh, into tajwid and your own voice, into one verse, kept. Bukhari records the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ saying: the best of you are those who learn the Qur'an and teach it. That's why the seven-year-old is on the carpet, and why a grandparent somewhere is listening. The juz' isn't the whole Qur'an. It's the doorway most people walk through. And now the path goes further in. Camp five has four strands: the most beautiful names of Allah, the Prophet's life in Medina, Rumi and the Sufi path for those who choose it, and how the Qur'an itself is built. Tomorrow we begin with the names.
screen: `HEARING, THEN REFUGE.` · `FROM AN-NAS BACK TO AN-NABA'.` · `CARRIED INTO PRAYER, SLEEP AND VOICE.` · `THE DOORWAY MOST PEOPLE WALK THROUGH.` · then, large: `THE ONES EVERY CHILD KNOWS.`

segments.voice: Sit the way that child sits, if your body lets you: cross-legged, back easy. Choose one surah you know by heart, or nearly. Al-Ikhlas is four lines. The Fatiha is seven. If you don't have a whole one yet, take the verse you kept yesterday. Now recite it from memory, without looking, slowly, in Arabic or in English. If you stumble, remember the two rewards, and keep going. When you finish, sit in the quiet and notice: this is in you now. The bell holds the time.
Camp four close. Seventy-five days through the thirtieth part, from An-Nas back to An-Naba', the surahs every Muslim child learns first. Today's word.
Your line: the ones every child knows. Today, say one surah by heart, and if there's a child or a friend who'd like to hear it, teach them one line. Day two hundred thirty-one.
